definition: Open-source intelligence: information gathered from publicly available sources, analysed for a specific question. Public does not mean harmless to collect: scope, purpose and law still apply.
Reading information that already exists in third-party records (DNS records, certificate logs, archives) without sending traffic to the target itself.

Sending traffic to the target (for example probing a port). It can alert the owner and needs written authorisation; in this app it is off unless an admin enables the active module and a scope authorisation exists.
Using one piece of data (an email, a domain) to find related data in another source.
Deciding who is behind an account, domain or activity. It needs independent corroboration; shared names and handles are not proof.
Support for a claim from an independent source (one that did not copy the first). Two sources that quote each other count as one.
A heuristic label (high/medium/low/unknown) with a reason. It is not a probability.
Where a piece of data came from: the tool, the time, the URL and the stored raw response with its hash.
A fingerprint of a file. If one bit changes, the fingerprint changes; the app re-checks it on every read.
The modern replacement for WHOIS: structured registration data for domains and IP ranges.
The older text protocol for domain registration records; many fields are redacted for privacy.
A = IPv4 address, AAAA = IPv6, MX = mail servers, NS = authoritative name servers, TXT = free text (SPF, verification tokens), CNAME = alias.
Public logs of issued TLS certificates (searched through crt.sh). They reveal hostnames a domain has had certificates for, including ones not linked anywhere.
Finding hostnames under a domain (api.example.com). Subfinder and Amass do this from public data sources; Amass needs data sources configured.
A historical record of which names pointed to which addresses, collected by third parties.
Metadata inside photos: camera, time, sometimes GPS position. It can be edited or missing; treat as a claim by the file.
Geospatial intelligence: positions, imagery and maps.
Signals intelligence. In this app only receive-only, owned or simulated radio data.
Human intelligence from people who consent. Recorded by alias only here.
Social-media intelligence, such as checking which sites have an account with a username (Sherlock, Maigret).
Checking many sites for an account named the same. A hit only shows that the name exists there, not that it is the same person.
A hash, domain, IP or URL associated with malicious activity.
A standard JSON format for sharing threat intelligence objects.
Software bill of materials: a list of components inside software.
ADS-B = aircraft position broadcasts; AIS = ship position broadcasts; NMEA = GPS receiver text format.
A format for recorded radio samples with metadata.
A network packet capture file. Import only captures you own; the app summarises it and never replays it.
The US SEC's company-filings database. The SEC asks API users to identify themselves, which is why Setup asks for a contact.
A government list of restricted persons or entities. Name matches are leads, not confirmations.
PUBLIC, INTERNAL, RESTRICTED or SECRET: how carefully the item must be handled in reports, AI and MCP.
How material was obtained: PUBLIC, OWNED_AUTHORIZED, CONSENTED, IMPORTED or SIMULATION.
A record of who handled evidence. The app records hashes and import events but its notes are not a legal certificate.
A proposed explanation. The app tallies supporting and contradicting claims; it never computes a probability.
A question the investigation needs answered.
Retrieval-augmented generation: the assistant is given the relevant documentation or evidence passages and must answer from them.
A community model with refusal behaviour removed from the weights. It is more willing to answer, so the app's own controls remain the gate.
A local program that runs open-weight language models on your computer.
A local inference engine for GGUF models, which can expose an OpenAI-compatible server on loopback.
An address that only your own computer can reach (127.0.0.1).
An encrypted SQLite database. The app's database is encrypted with it.
Model Context Protocol: a standard for letting an AI client use tools. Here it is read-only unless you approve a change.
Active Intelligence and Verification: bounded, disclosed checks (HTTP headers, TLS, a few ports, approved read-only signatures) of assets someone authorized. Not exploitation, not credential testing.
Permission from whoever owns or controls a host, naming the hosts, ports, checks, an end date and the proof. It is separate from a person's consent to be researched.
A fingerprint of an exact verification plan, its authorization scope, limits and tool versions. An approval applies to one hash only; any edit needs a new approval.
Defensive exposure intelligence: provider-reported breaches, dark-web mentions and ransomware listings for yourself, verified clients and authorized organizations.
A way to check a password against known breaches by sending only the first five characters of its hash. The application relays those five characters and keeps nothing.
No provider has been asked. It is never the same as 'no exposure'.
The named providers reported nothing at the times shown. It does not show an identifier was never exposed.
A provider or leak-site claim. A listing is not proof that data exists, is accurate or is still reachable.
An address a source associates with the target. It is a candidate until a person confirms it; guessed patterns are never presented as discoveries.
Likely: two independent sources explicitly tie an address to the subject. Possible: seen in evidence but not tied by enough independent sources, or the evidence conflicts. Neither is a fact.
The prioritized, inspectable list of research steps that start from your inputs and confirmed addresses, across disciplines, inside depth, budget and authorization limits.
A value that rests only on the subject's own statement. It is recorded as such and is never counted as independent corroboration.

Looking up an exact email address in public references (a public profile, a code-hosting search, a key server, an optional keyed web search). It never treats the address's domain as something the subject owns, and it never probes password-reset or login pages.
A domain such as gmail.com that thousands of unrelated people use. An address there says nothing about who owns the domain, so domain, DNS and certificate lookups are never run from it.
